sweep_summary: Two title-hits for Russian. (1) Melvold 1990 (MIT PhD, already listed) was previously unfetchable (DSpace /download URL is WAF-blocked, not reachable by automated download); It states that Russian stress is set by lexically-determined accentual properties of morphemes plus the Basic Accentuation Principle (stress the leftmost accented vowel; if none, the initial vowel), with ~90% of nouns stem-fixed and the rest ending-fixed, mobile or shifting (pp. 12-13, 13, 16, 39). This confirms the catalog's 'lexical' coding and is a better deciding source than Forbes 1917 (a pedagogical grammar that declines to state the rules); it also agrees with the JIPA illustration (Yanushevskaya & Buncic 2015 p. 225, downloaded 2026-09-16: 'The stress is free and can fall on any syllable'). (2) Lagerberg 1999 (Astra Press, Birmingham; ISBN 9780946134564, OCLC 40981436) is about stress in Russian suffixed derivatives but has no open copy: HathiTrust is search-only (mdp.39015042995749, rights ic), Google Books has no preview, no DOI; print only, medium priority (specialised, not the best general stress statement). with file -> citation -> URL) and an addendum

new_statements.reading: Russian word stress is lexically determined: each morpheme is underlyingly accented or unaccented, and a single word stress surfaces on the leftmost lexically accented vowel; only when a word has no accented morpheme does a positional default (initial syllable) apply. Stem-fixed stress covers about 90% of dictionary nouns; ending-fixed, initial/final mobile and final/penult shifting patterns account for the rest. This confirms the catalog's 'lexical' coding and refines it by naming the mechanism (lexical accent + leftmost-accent rule, initial default), which the Forbes 1917 quote ('mobile, i.e. it can fall on any syllable.. rules.. riddled with exceptions') only gestures

(2) The deciding source is a 1917 pedagogical grammar; it is not the best available description (Timberlake 2004 CUP reference grammar, Halle 1973, Melvold 1990, Zaliznjak 1985, JIPA 2015 all exist), but the fact coded — free, lexically determined, paradigmatically mobile stress with no weight criterion — is among the least controversial facts in stress typology and every later source agrees. sources.quote: In this chapter I will show that the stress system of Russian involves the interaction between lexically-determined accentual properties of morphemes and a rule which assigns stress to the leftmost accented vowel or, in the absence of an accent, to the leftmost vowel. (pp. 12-13) ... (4) Basic Accentuation Principle (BAP): Assign stress to the leftmost accented vowel; if there is no accented vowel, assign stress to the initial vowel. (p. 16) ... (i) FIXED ON THE STEM ... About 90% of the nouns in the Russian dictionary exhibit this stress pattern. (ii) FIXED ON THE INFLECTION ... approximate number: 2,000 (iii) ALTERNATING BETWEEN THE INITIAL AND FINAL VOWEL ... 450 (iv) ALTERNATING BETWEEN THE FINAL AND PENULTIMATE VOWEL ... 250 (p. 13)
sources.locator: pp. 12-13 (end of §1.1); p. 13 table (2) 'Four Main Types of Nominal Stress'; p. 16 rule (4) Basic Accentuation Principle; p. 39
sources.note: Russian has an accent-based (lexical-accent) stress system: morphemes are lexically [+/-accented, +/-dominant]; a cyclic rule (Kiparsky-Halle Basic Accentuation Principle) places the single word stress on the leftmost accented vowel, defaulting to the initial vowel when no morpheme is accented. Four nominal patterns: stem-fixed (~90% of dictionary nouns), ending-fixed, initial/final mobile, final/penult shifting. Stress position is therefore lexically determined (not predictable from syllable count or weight), with an initial-syllable default.

sources.quote: 'The prominence of the stressed syllable in Russian is achieved primarily through the duration and quality of the stressed vowel ... The stress is free and can fall on any syllable in a word. In the majority of cases, the stress is stable, that is it falls on the same syllable in the word within its paradigm or in its derivatives, e.g. brat'ja ... There is, however, a large number of common words where the stress moves within the word's paradigm or in derived forms, e.g. gorod [ˈɡ...] "city" but goroda [...ˈda] "cities" (Bondarko 1998).' No weight criterion; secondary stress not discussed.
